316.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
316.hook: a sixteen-year-old in Madurai lies down on the floor and acts out his own death
316.tomorrow: karma: seva, and a word Ramakrishna refused
316.howItsDone: Visitors to Ramana Maharshi's ashram at Tiruvannamalai sit in silence in his old hall and walk around the hill of Arunachala; followers practice self-inquiry by turning attention to the sense of I rather than to its thoughts.

segments.voice: Last week closed on three roads: karma with Vivekananda, bhakti with Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, jnana with I am Brahman. Sometimes God bows. This week, a new teacher on the jnana road.

Madurai, South India, the summer of 1896. A sixteen-year-old boy named Venkataraman is alone in a room in his uncle's house. He's healthy. Nothing is wrong. Suddenly an overwhelming fear hits him: he's about to die. He could call someone, or go for a walk. He does something else. He lies down on the floor, stretches out his limbs like a corpse, holds his breath, and says to himself: all right. Death has come. What does it mean? What is it that's dying?
screen: `MADURAI, 1896.` → `A SUDDEN FEAR OF DEATH.` → `HE LIES DOWN AND ASKS.`

segments.voice: Lying there, as he later told it, he reasoned it through. This body is dead. They'll carry it to the cremation ground and burn it. But with the body dead, am I dead? Is the body I? And in that moment, he said, he knew directly that he was not the body: the I, the Self, was something the body's death couldn't touch. The fear vanished and never came back. A few weeks later he left home with a short note and took a train toward a sacred mountain called Arunachala, in the town of Tiruvannamalai. He stayed at that mountain for the rest of his life, more than fifty years. People came to call him Ramana Maharshi, and they came from far away to sit with him. Often he said nothing at all. When he did teach, the heart of it was a single question: who am I? Not a riddle to answer with words. Not I'm a teacher, I'm a parent, I'm tired. Those are things you have, he'd say, in effect, not what you are. Instead, follow the feeling of I back to where it comes from. That's self-inquiry: the jnana road with almost nothing extra. No ritual required, no long study, just attention turned toward its source. What he did at sixteen on that floor, he spent fifty years inviting others to try, gently, from wherever they were.
screen: `THE BODY DIES. AM I DEAD?` · `THE FEAR NEVER CAME BACK.` · `FIFTY YEARS AT ARUNACHALA.` · `ONE QUESTION: WHO AM I?` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Ask the question once, quietly: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a role; just notice the plain sense of being here, this I that's listening, and when a thought comes, let it pass and come back to the question. Rest in the space where the answer would be; it's fine if nothing happens, because the looking is the practice, and if you pray, you can rest in God as the source of that I.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action was to lie down and look, and he spent his life inviting others to turn and look too.
Your line: who am I? Not a name, not a job: just the one asking. See you tomorrow.

317.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
317.hook: a teacher hears the word compassion and stops the room: who are you to be compassionate?
317.tomorrow: bhakti: Radha in the spring forest
317.howItsDone: Seva is practiced in Hindu temples as service to the deity and to devotees, cleaning, cooking and serving food, and the Ramakrishna Mission and many other Hindu organizations run hospitals, schools and relief work as seva, serving people as God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: Ramana Maharshi, sixteen, on the floor, asking who am I. Today the karma road reaches its last stretch: seva as a life.

A charity photo: someone well dressed hands a meal to someone who isn't. Both smile for the camera, and the picture still says who's above and who's below. Now a temple garden at Dakshineswar, near Calcutta, in the 1880s. A small group of young men sits around their teacher, Ramakrishna, and someone mentions a teaching about showing compassion to all living beings. It sounds beautiful. And Ramakrishna, the story goes, stops the room.
screen: `THE CHARITY PHOTO.` → `A TEMPLE GARDEN, THE 1880S.` → `RAMAKRISHNA STOPS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Compassion to beings? he says. Who are you to show compassion? You, a tiny creature, being kind to others as if from above? No. Not compassion. Service. Serve every being as Shiva himself. In Bengali the phrase is often given as shiva jnane jiva seva: serving living beings, knowing them as God. In the room was a young man named Narendranath, who would become Swami Vivekananda. As his fellow disciples told it, he walked out afterward and said something like: I've found a great light today, and if God lets me, I'll proclaim it everywhere. And he did. When he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, he gave it a motto that joins two things: for one's own liberation, and for the good of the world. The word seva is older than any of them, from a Sanskrit root that means to attend on, to honor, to serve. In a temple, seva is what you do for the image of God: bathing it, dressing it, offering food. Ramakrishna pointed that same word outward. The hungry person in front of you gets the same care as the image in the shrine. Now look at the charity photo again. There's no above and below. The one serving stands where a worshiper stands. Seva isn't volunteering on the side of your spiritual life. On the karma road, it is the spiritual life.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU TO SHOW COMPASSION?` · `SERVE EVERY BEING AS SHIVA.` · `A YOUNG MAN SAW A GREAT LIGHT.` · `NO ABOVE, NO BELOW.` · then, large: `SHIVA JNANE JIVA SEVA.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you'll likely help today in any small way, a kid, a coworker, a stranger at a counter, an aging parent, and notice any feeling of being above them, even slightly: the helper, the one who has it together. Let it go with the out-breath, and picture serving them the way you'd offer something at a shrine: carefully, gladly, as if it were an honor. If you pray, you can ask to see God in them.
Karma. Action. On the karma road's last stretch, the action is seva: service offered to beings as if to God.
Your line: serve every being as Shiva. Ramakrishna carried a temple word out into the street. Day three hundred seventeen.

318.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
318.hook: spring in the forest, Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone else, and a friend steps in
318.tomorrow: jnana: to whom did this thought come?
318.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda's songs are sung in temples and at home, and its opening hymn to Vishnu's ten avatars is often sung on its own; in Vaishnava traditions devotees honor the sakhis, Radha's friends, as models of selfless devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: seva, not compassion from above, but serve every being as Shiva. Today, back into Jayadeva's poem.

Someone walks into a party looking for one person, and there they are: laughing, surrounded, completely fine. Nobody did anything wrong, exactly. But leaving suddenly looks easier than staying. That's where Jayadeva's poem puts Radha. It's spring in the forest by the Yamuna. Bees, blossoms, a warm wind from the south. Radha's friend leads her to a clearing and points: there's Krishna, dancing and playing with all the other gopis.
screen: `LOOKING FOR ONE PERSON.` → `SPRING BY THE YAMUNA.` → `KRISHNA, WITH EVERYONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Radha doesn't make a scene. She withdraws, alone into a thicket of vines, hurt and jealous and full of longing all at once. Then the poem does something interesting. Krishna, in the middle of the dance, suddenly remembers her. He leaves the others to look for her, can't find her, and now he's the miserable one. So they're apart, each longing for the other, and neither can simply walk across the forest and fix it. That's when Radha's friend, the sakhi, gets to work. She goes to Krishna and describes Radha's grief. She goes back to Radha and tells her how Krishna is suffering. Back and forth, carrying the messages, softening the hurt, until the two can meet again. Devotees hear layers in this. Krishna dancing with everyone is God's love for all souls. Radha's hurt is the soul feeling, for a moment, like one among many. Krishna's search says God is not fine without you after all. And the sakhi? In some Vaishnava traditions, devotees see her as the model of what a teacher or a community does: the friend who carries messages between the soul and God. Some traditions go further and hope for nothing more than to be that friend, serving the love between Radha and Krishna. One more thing: the poem opens with a hymn to Vishnu's ten descents into the world, and people still sing it on its own.
screen: `RADHA WITHDRAWS, HURT.` · `KRISHNA LEAVES THE DANCE TO FIND HER.` · `THE FRIEND CARRIES THE MESSAGES.` · `GOD IS NOT FINE WITHOUT YOU.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who once carried a message for you: a friend who explained you to someone you'd hurt, a teacher who helped you back to something you'd lost, a grandparent who made peace in the family. Picture them, and thank them silently. If you pray, you can thank God for the friends who stood between.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the Gita Govinda, the action that heals is the friend's: going back and forth until two can meet.
Your line: the friend between them. Two lovers, one forest, and a friend going back and forth. That's three hundred eighteen days.

319.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
319.hook: don't fight the thought and don't follow it: ask who it came to
319.tomorrow: karma: the right kind of gift
319.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry in daily life and in silent sitting, turning each thought back with the question 'to whom?'; many combine it with devotion, as Ramana allowed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: Radha hurt in the spring forest, Krishna searching, and the friend between them, carrying the messages. Today, Ramana's method, up close.

You sit down to be quiet for two minutes, and within five seconds your mind is planning dinner. You come back, and now it's replaying something someone said on Tuesday. Most advice gives you two options. Fight the thought: push it away, clear your mind. Or follow it, and end up twenty minutes deep in Tuesday. Ramana Maharshi, the sage of Arunachala, offered a third move. It fits in one sentence, and people spend their lives on it.
screen: `FIVE SECONDS IN: DINNER.` → `FIGHT IT, OR FOLLOW IT?` → `A THIRD MOVE.`

segments.voice: It's in his little teaching called Who Am I? When a thought arises, he says, in effect, don't chase it, and don't wrestle it. Ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer comes back instantly: to me. Then ask: and who am I? In that moment, the attention turns around. Instead of flowing out toward dinner or Tuesday, it flows back toward its own source, and the thought you started with drops away, because nobody's feeding it. His reasoning: of all the thoughts in the mind, the thought I is the first. Every other thought is a thought to someone: I'm hungry, I'm annoyed, I remember. Trace I back, and every other thought loses its root. He gave a vivid picture from the cremation ground. A stick is used to stir the cremation fire. It keeps the fire going, and at the end, the stick itself is thrown into the flames. The question who am I works like that stick. It stirs up and burns away all the other thoughts, and in the end it burns away too, leaving only what was there all along. Ramana was also generous about other roads. If you can't inquire, he said, then surrender completely to God; both lead to the same place. That's a jnana teacher honoring the bhakti road. And his method is portable. No temple, no teacher in the room, not a single book. Just the next thought, and one question.
screen: `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.` · `AND WHO AM I?` · `EVERY THOUGHT IS A THOUGHT TO SOMEONE.` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE BURNS TOO.` · then, large: `TO WHOM?`

segments.voice: Let thoughts come as they will, and when one appears, don't push it away or follow it; ask quietly: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I? Let the attention rest wherever it lands, without needing an answer, and ask again with the next thought; ten times in two minutes is the practice working. If surrender suits you better, as Ramana allowed, you can simply hand each thought to God instead.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action is the smallest one on the path: one question, turned back toward the one who asks.
Your line: ask the thought, to whom? Ramana's whole method fits in those three words. Day three hundred nineteen, done.

320.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
320.hook: two people give the same gift, and the Gita says they gave completely different things
320.carry: give with faith, and tell no one
320.howItsDone: Dana, giving, is a daily and festival duty in many Hindu homes, food to the hungry, gifts to temples and to those in need, and Gita 17.20–17.22 and the Taittiriya Upanishad's 'give with faith' are often quoted to describe how a gift should be given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: ask the thought, to whom? Today the karma road, and seva as a whole life, starting with how you give.

Two people give the same amount to the same cause on the same day. One does it quietly and never mentions it. The other makes sure their name is on the plaque, posts the receipt, and brings it up at dinner for a month. Same money. Same cause. Did they give the same thing? The Gita takes up that question in its seventeenth chapter, and its answer has nothing to do with the amount. A gift, it says, comes in three kinds.
screen: `SAME AMOUNT, SAME CAUSE.` → `ONE QUIET, ONE ON A PLAQUE.` → `THREE KINDS OF GIFT.`

segments.voice: It uses the three gunas you met with Patanjali: clarity, restlessness and heaviness. The clear gift, Krishna says, is given simply because giving is right, to someone who can't pay you back, at the right place and time, to the right person. The restless gift is given expecting something in return, or for the reward it'll bring, or grudgingly, with a wince. The heavy gift is given at the wrong time and place, to the wrong person, without respect, even with contempt. So the line isn't how much you give. It's what's in the hand along with it. The Taittiriya Upanishad, advising students as they leave their teacher's home, says it in short commands. Give with faith. Don't give without faith. Give generously. Give with modesty. Give with awe. Give with understanding. In Sanskrit, the first is shraddhaya deyam: give with faith. That's seva as a life: not a big gesture once a year, but a thousand small gifts, a meal, an hour, a ride, a listening ear, each given the clear way. Not to be seen. Not to be repaid. Not with a sigh. The Gita's wider teaching adds a reason: again and again, it says that action done without craving for its fruit doesn't bind the one who acts. The restless gift is still waiting for its thanks. The clear gift leaves the hand, and it's finished. The Gita's word for a gift is dana. On the karma road, a life of seva is a life of dana, given clearly.
screen: `GIVEN BECAUSE IT'S RIGHT.` · `GIVEN FOR RETURN, OR GRUDGINGLY.` · `GIVEN WITH CONTEMPT.` · `IT'S WHAT'S IN THE HAND WITH IT.` · then, large: `ŚRADDHAYĀ DEYAM.`

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you gave, money, time, a favor, a meal, and look honestly and gently: was there a hope for thanks in it, a little wince? That's fine; everyone's gifts are mixed. Then remember a gift you gave that was clean, no strings, no sigh, notice what that one was like, and let it be enough; if you pray, you can offer your giving to God, mixed as it is.
Karma. Action. In the Gita's seventeenth chapter, the action of giving comes in three kinds, and the clear one is given simply because giving is right.
Your line: give with faith, and tell no one. The clear gift isn't waiting for its thanks. See you tomorrow.

321.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda has long been sung in the worship of Jagannath at Puri and is performed in Odissi and other classical dance and music; devotees hear its reunion of Radha and Krishna as the soul's union with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: three kinds of gift, and the clear one that leaves the hand, finished. Today, the bhakti road's last day with Jayadeva.

A wedding. A kiss in the rain. Credits roll. That's where a lot of love stories stop. Jayadeva's Gita Govinda ends somewhere much quieter. After the hurt and the searching and the messages carried back and forth, after Krishna has pleaded with Radha to forgive him, she finally comes to him in the forest bower at night. And in the poem's very last song, the morning after, Radha asks Krishna for something small. Fix my hair, she says. Put my ornaments back. And he does.
screen: `NOT A WEDDING. NOT CREDITS.` → `RADHA COMES TO THE BOWER.` → `FIX MY HAIR, SHE SAYS.`

segments.voice: Here is the Lord of the universe, the cowherd whose flute the gopis ran to, the child who showed the whole cosmos in his mouth, sitting in the grass, carefully drawing the line of dark makeup around Radha's eyes, pinning flowers back into her hair, fastening her anklets. That's the poem's last image. Remember the line tradition says Jayadeva hesitated to write, where Krishna asks Radha to put her foot on his head? The ending finishes that thought. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the one who is served. God serves. In the reunion, the Lord does seva for the one who loves him. And that brings the three roads together in a way you might not expect. This week the karma road has been about seva: serving every being as God. In the Gita Govinda, God serves the soul. The service goes both ways. The poem didn't stay on the page. Tradition says its songs were sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and temple dancers performed them; Odissi dancers still do. Singers perform its songs, the ashtapadis, each one built of eight verses. People who can't read a word of Sanskrit know its melodies. Tomorrow the three roads end together. Today, the bhakti road leaves you with Krishna in the grass, making someone he loves beautiful again. On this road, that's what love finally looks like. Not winning. Tending.
screen: `THE LORD FIXES RADHA'S HAIR.` · `GOD SERVES THE ONE WHO LOVES HIM.` · `SEVA GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `SUNG IN WORSHIP AT PURI.` · then, large: `NOT WINNING. TENDING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who once tended to you in a small, physical way: brushed your hair when you were little, fixed your collar before something important, brought you soup. Picture their hands, and receive that care again as you breathe in. If you pray, you can rest in being tended by God.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and the Gita Govinda ends with a small, gentle action: God tending the one he loves.
Your line: tending, not winning. The poem ends on flowers pinned back in her hair. That's day three hundred twenty-one.

322.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
322.hook: three weeks, three tracks, one last day on each: the kitchen, the song and the question
322.carry: serving, singing, asking: all a doing
322.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Sikh means by seva
322.howItsDone: Hindus often speak of three great paths: karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge). People often lean toward one, and some teachers say the paths meet; schools differ on how.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tending, not winning, as Krishna fixed Radha's hair. Today the three tracks end: karma, bhakti, jnana.

Three people, the same evening. One is at a community kitchen, sleeves rolled up, ladling dal for strangers; she stopped counting the hours long ago. One is on a floor cushion with an old book of love songs, reading one verse twice, too beautiful to leave. One sits in a quiet room, eyes closed, asking a question so simple it's almost rude: who is it that's sitting here? Three weeks ago you picked one of them to walk beside. Today all three get to speak.
screen: `THE KITCHEN.` → `THE SONG.` → `THE QUESTION.` → `THE LAST DAY OF THE TRACK.`

segments.voice: The kitchen first. The karma track ended in seva as a life: service with no bill attached. Not a weekend of volunteering: every job, paid or unpaid, as an offering. The Gita's third chapter said it; Vivekananda said it in New York; people on this track still say it with a ladle in hand. Then the song. The bhakti track ended in the Gita Govinda, Jayadeva's Sanskrit poem of Radha and Krishna: longing, a quarrel, a reunion in a forest by the river. Tradition says it has been sung at the Jagannath temple in Puri for centuries, and dancers across India still perform it. Devotees hear the love story as the soul's longing for God. Then the question. The jnana track ended with Ramana Maharshi, who, the story goes, lay down as a young man and asked what dies when the body dies. He spent the rest of his life at the hill of Arunachala, and his teaching fits in three words: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a job, he said, in effect. Follow the thought I back to where it rises, and rest there. Yet the Gita's fifth chapter says of the way of knowledge and the way of action: it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of them as separate. Some teachers hear that as true of all three ways. Hindus have long argued about how the paths fit together, and they still do; this path doesn't settle it. It just notices that all three begin with the same small word: karma. The ladle is a doing. The song is a doing. Even the question is a doing.
screen: `KARMA: SEVA AS A LIFE.` · `BHAKTI: THE GITA GOVINDA.` · `JNANA: RAMANA'S WHO AM I?` · `ALL THREE BEGIN WITH A DOING.` · then, large: `KARMA.`

segments.voice: Let the track you walked come back to you: for the kitchen, one piece of work you did this month for someone else; for the song, a line or a name you love; for the question, let the word I rise and gently look for where it comes from. If you didn't pick a track at all, just watch the breath; it's a doing too. No grade, no finish line.
Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first name on three tracks, and the ground under them all.
Your line: serving, singing, asking: all a doing. Day three hundred twenty-two: three tracks, done.
